seo.title: uv Python Tutorial #11 — Why uv Is Actually This Fast (2026)
altTitles: The uv cache explained: buckets, keys, hard links and prune
seo.description: Chapter eleven of the uv course. What the uv cache keeps and how each bucket is keyed, why built wheels matter, hard linking, cache-keys, uv cache prune and prune --ci, and an honest look at where the speed numbers actually come from.

scenes.narration: Five point seven seconds. Then nought point two nine. Same command, same machine.

scenes.narration: Welcome back. This chapter is the honest answer to why uv feels the way it does — not a benchmark graphic, but the actual mechanism, and what it costs you in disk space.

data.title: Why it is this fast
data.subtitle: uv, chapter eleven · the depot, and the honest numbers

scenes.narration: Start with what actually gets kept, because the answer is more than you'd guess.

The cache is a folder of buckets, and each bucket holds a different kind of thing. Downloaded archives. Built wheels. Source distributions. Whole environments, from chapter two. And every bucket carries a version number in its name, which means several uv releases can share one cache without ever confusing each other.

uvStage.headline: Buckets, and [version] numbers
uvStage.premise: One folder per kind of thing, each versioned so several uv releases can share.

steps.label: ls "$(uv cache dir)"
steps.detail: the trailing number is the format version

stage.label: archive-v0/
stage.sub: what was downloaded

stage.label: wheels-v6/
stage.sub: and what was built from it

stage.label: sdists-v9/
stage.sub: source distributions, unpacked

stage.label: environments-v2/
stage.sub: the throwaway envs from chapter two

scenes.narration: The built wheels bucket is the one that matters most. Some packages contain C code that has to be compiled, and compiling can take minutes. uv keeps the compiled result, so the second time you need that package on this machine, there is nothing to compile at all.

uvStage.headline: It keeps what it [built], too
uvStage.premise: Compiling C extensions takes minutes. uv keeps the result and never repeats it.

steps.label: time uv add some-c-extension
steps.detail: a minute and a quarter of compiling

steps.label: time uv add some-c-extension
steps.detail: and nothing at all to compile this time

stage.label: first build
stage.sub: the compiler actually ran

stage.label: second time
stage.sub: the built wheel was already there

stage.label: and every project after it, too

scenes.narration: Each kind of thing is keyed on whatever identifies it. A registry download is keyed on the URL and the response headers. A git dependency is keyed on the commit hash, which is exactly right — a branch moves, a commit never does. And a local folder is keyed on the modification time of its files.

uvStage.headline: Keyed on what [identifies] it
uvStage.premise: Each source has a natural identity, and uv keys the cache entry on that.

steps.label: ls "$(uv cache dir)/environments-v2" | head -2
steps.detail: the suffix is the key, hashed

stage.label: from the registry
stage.sub: plus the caching headers it sent

stage.label: from git
stage.sub: a branch moves; a commit cannot

stage.label: from a folder
stage.sub: when the files last changed

stage.label: an immutable file
stage.sub: a versioned filename never changes

scenes.narration: And when the default key isn't right, you can say so. Cache-keys in pyproject lets you tell uv what a rebuild actually depends on — a particular file, a git commit, an environment variable — so your builds neither rebuild pointlessly nor skip a rebuild they needed.

uvStage.headline: Tell it what a rebuild [depends on]
uvStage.premise: cache-keys names what should invalidate a build, when the default guess is wrong.

steps.label: grep -A4 cache-keys pyproject.toml
steps.detail: rebuild when these change, and only then

scenes.narration: So the cache explains the second run. But the first run was fast too. Why?

Three other things are doing work here. uv is compiled, which means no interpreter has to start up before anything can happen. uv downloads and installs in parallel rather than one package after another, so a slow package never blocks a fast one. And where the operating system allows it, uv hard-links files into place instead of copying them.

uvStage.headline: Compiled, parallel, [linked]
uvStage.premise: Three things beyond the cache: no interpreter start, parallel work, hard links.

steps.label: time uv sync
steps.detail: thirteen packages, forty-seven milliseconds

stage.label: compiled
stage.sub: nothing to interpret before starting

stage.label: parallel
stage.sub: not one package after another

scenes.narration: Hard linking deserves a sentence, because it sounds like cheating and isn't. A hard link is a second name for a file that already exists on disk. So installing a cached package into a new environment writes almost no bytes — the file is already there, and the environment just points at it.

uvStage.headline: A second [name], not a copy
uvStage.premise: A hard link is another name for bytes already on disk. Nothing is written twice.

steps.label: du -sh invoice-app/.venv report-tool/.venv
steps.detail: and the disk did not lose eight megabytes

stage.label: pygments
stage.sub: on disk once, named from both places

scenes.narration: Now let's be careful about numbers, because this is where tutorials get sloppy. Astral's homepage says ten to a hundred times faster than pip. That's their claim, and I'm attributing it rather than repeating it as fact. Their own benchmarks page, at the time of recording, carries no figures at all.

uvStage.headline: Where the [numbers] come from
uvStage.premise: One claim from a homepage, one pair measured here. They are not the same thing.

steps.label: time uvx ruff --version
steps.detail: this one I measured, on this machine

stage.label: Astral's homepage
stage.sub: their claim, not my measurement

stage.label: this machine
stage.sub: 5.792s to 0.294s, measured here

scenes.narration: The honest version is simpler, and more useful anyway. On a cold cache uv is roughly as fast as your internet connection allows, because there's genuinely nothing else to wait for. On a warm cache uv is roughly as fast as your disk allows. Which is why the first install of the day feels ordinary and everything afterwards feels instant.

uvStage.headline: Network-bound, then [disk-bound]
uvStage.premise: Cold, you wait for the network. Warm, you wait for the disk. Nothing else.

steps.label: time uv sync --refresh
steps.detail: cold: waiting for the network

steps.label: time uv sync
steps.detail: warm: waiting for almost nothing

stage.label: cold
stage.sub: as fast as your connection allows

stage.label: warm
stage.sub: as fast as your disk allows

stage.label: and that is the whole trick

scenes.narration: All of which costs disk space, so let's look at managing it.

Four commands, and each does something different. Dir tells you where the cache is. Clean empties the whole thing, or one named package. Prune removes only what nothing needs any more. And prune with the CI flag is tuned for build machines, where keeping built wheels is wasteful.

uvStage.headline: Four commands, [four] jobs
uvStage.premise: Empty it, empty part of it, tidy it, or tidy it the way a build machine wants.

steps.label: uv cache dir && du -sh "$(uv cache dir)"
steps.detail: four hundred megabytes, well spent

steps.label: uv cache clean ruff
steps.detail: one package, when you suspect a stale copy

steps.label: uv cache prune
steps.detail: only what nothing needs any more

scenes.narration: The CI variant is worth knowing if you run builds. On a build machine the cache usually lives in a saved archive, and built wheels are expensive to store but cheap to rebuild — so keeping them is the wrong trade. Prune with the CI flag keeps the downloads and discards the wheels, which means the saved archive gets dramatically smaller.

uvStage.headline: A [smaller] cache, for CI
uvStage.premise: On a build machine, storing built wheels costs more than rebuilding them.

steps.label: du -sh "$(uv cache dir)" && uv cache prune --ci
steps.detail: the wheels go; the downloads stay

steps.label: du -sh "$(uv cache dir)"
steps.detail: a much cheaper thing to save and restore

stage.label: before
stage.sub: downloads plus everything built

stage.label: after --ci
stage.sub: downloads only, wheels discarded

stage.label: cheaper to store, and quick to rebuild

scenes.narration: One thing the cache is not is a mirror. uv still asks the index whether anything has changed, using the ordinary caching headers every web server understands. So a cached copy is used because the server said the copy is still current, not because uv decided to stop checking.

uvStage.headline: It still [asks] the index
uvStage.premise: A cached copy is used because the server said so, not because uv stopped asking.

steps.label: uv sync -v 2>&1 | grep -i "cached\|304" | head -2
steps.detail: fresh means the server confirmed it

stage.label: a question
stage.sub: has anything changed since last time?

stage.label: the answer
stage.sub: so the depot copy is used

scenes.narration: That also explains a failure mode worth recognising. If a cached copy ever seems stale or wrong, you don't need to delete the whole cache and start again. Refresh forces one command past the depot, and cache clean with a package name removes exactly that package's entries.

uvStage.headline: Suspect it? Do the [small] thing
uvStage.premise: Two narrow tools before the blunt one. Emptying the whole cache is rarely needed.

steps.label: uv sync --refresh-package rich
steps.detail: one package, past the depot, once

steps.label: uv cache clean rich
steps.detail: or evict just that package permanently

stage.label: --refresh-package
stage.sub: one command, one package

stage.label: uv cache clean
stage.sub: four hundred megabytes, gone

scenes.narration: And a practical note if your machine is short of space. The cache and your project folders should live on the same filesystem, because hard linking only works within one filesystem. Put them on different disks and uv falls back to copying, which costs both time and space.

uvStage.headline: Keep them on [one] disk
uvStage.premise: Hard links only work within a filesystem. Across two, uv has to copy instead.

steps.label: df --output=source "$(uv cache dir)" ~/work | tail -2
steps.detail: same filesystem, so links are possible

stage.label: wall
stage.sub: a link cannot cross a filesystem boundary

scenes.narration: Quick check. What makes the second uvx run so much faster than the first? Pause the video here and answer it for yourself before I do. Ready? The cache. The parcel was already in the local depot, so nothing had to be fetched or built again.

quiz.question: Why is the second uvx run so much faster?

options.text: uv warms up as it runs

quiz.why: Nothing was fetched and nothing was built. The depot already had it.

scenes.narration: So, to recap. uv keeps what it downloaded and what it built, keyed on whatever identifies each thing. Being compiled, working in parallel and hard-linking explain the rest. And the only figures worth quoting are the ones you measured yourself.

points.text: It keeps downloads AND built wheels
